focus: Matthew 5 opens the Sermon on the Mount as Jesus, seated on a mountain, teaches His disciples while the multitudes listen. He pronounces the blessedness of those who belong to the kingdom, calls them the salt of the earth and the light of the world, declares that He came not to destroy the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them, and then, in six contrasts introduced by “But I say to you,” brings God’s commands to bear on anger, lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love for enemies.

sections.title: The Beatitudes
sections.summary: Seeing the multitudes, Jesus goes up on a mountain and teaches His disciples, pronouncing blessed the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness’ sake. He tells His disciples to rejoice when they are reviled and persecuted for His sake, for great is their reward in heaven.

sections.title: Salt of the Earth and Light of the World
sections.summary: Jesus tells His disciples, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13), warning that salt which loses its flavor is good for nothing. He also calls them the light of the world and tells them to let their light shine before men, so that people may see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven.

sections.title: Jesus Fulfills the Law and the Prophets
sections.summary: Jesus declares, “I did not come to destroy but to fulfill” (Matthew 5:17), and affirms that not one jot or tittle will pass from the law till all is fulfilled. Whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, and whoever does and teaches them will be called great, but unless His hearers’ righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will by no means enter it.

sections.title: Anger, Contempt, and Reconciliation
sections.summary: Jesus brings the command against murder to bear on anger and contemptuous words, warning that these deserve judgment. He tells His hearers to be reconciled with a brother before offering a gift at the altar and to agree quickly with an adversary on the way to court.

sections.title: Lust and Decisive Removal of Sin
sections.summary: Jesus declares that whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. With the vivid picture of plucking out a right eye or cutting off a right hand, Jesus calls His hearers to remove decisively whatever leads them into sin, for it is better to lose one member than for the whole body to be cast into hell.

sections.title: Divorce
sections.summary: Jesus sets the law’s provision for a certificate of divorce beside His own word. Whoever divorces his wife for any reason except sexual immorality causes her to commit adultery, and whoever marries a woman who is divorced commits adultery.

sections.title: Oaths and Truthful Speech
sections.summary: Jesus confronts the evasive use of oaths in ordinary speech, forbidding swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one’s own head, for each belongs to God or lies beyond human control. Instead His disciples are to let their “Yes” be “Yes” and their “No” be “No,” since whatever is more than these is from the evil one.

sections.title: Yielding the Right to Retaliate
sections.summary: Against the principle of “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (Matthew 5:38), Jesus tells His hearers not to resist an evil person but to turn the other cheek, give up their cloak, and go the second mile. They are to give to the one who asks and not turn away the one who wants to borrow.

sections.title: Love for Enemies
sections.summary: Jesus commands His hearers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, so that they may be sons of their Father in heaven, who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good alike. Loving only those who love them is no more than tax collectors do, and Jesus concludes, “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48).

1.brief: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up on a mountain and sits down, and His disciples come to Him. He takes the teacher’s seated posture to instruct His followers, while the crowds listen in.
1.explain:
“And seeing the multitudes,”

The multitudes are the crowds of 4:25, drawn by Jesus’ preaching and especially by His healings. Jesus sees them, and His response is to teach. The crowds do not disappear. They remain within hearing, and at the end of the sermon Matthew reports that “the people were astonished at His teaching” (7:28).

Matthew has just summarized Jesus’ ministry of teaching, preaching, and healing throughout Galilee (4:23–25). Great crowds now follow Him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan. The Sermon on the Mount opens against that background.

“He went up on a mountain,”

Matthew does not name the mountain. Tradition places it on the hills above the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, where Jesus had made His home (4:13). For Jewish readers, the picture of God’s instruction being given from a mountain would naturally recall Moses at Sinai (Exodus 19–20). Matthew has already shown Jesus retracing Israel’s story: going down to Egypt and coming out again (2:15), passing through the waters (3:13–17), and being tested in the wilderness (4:1–11). Now He ascends a mountain and explains the true meaning of God’s law (5:17–48), not as a second Moses who receives it but as the One who speaks with authority of His own.

“and when He was seated”

Jewish teachers customarily sat to teach (Luke 4:20–21; Matthew 23:2). Jesus’ sitting signals formal, deliberate instruction rather than passing remarks.

“His disciples came to Him.”

“Disciples” here refers to a wider circle than the Twelve, who have not yet been named (10:1–4). Only four have been called so far (4:18–22). The teaching is directed first to those who have begun to follow Jesus, with the crowds listening at the edges. The Sermon describes the life of people who already belong to the kingdom, not a list of conditions for strangers to meet.
1.notes:
Luke records similar teaching given on “a level place” (Luke 6:17–49). Some understand this as the same occasion, a level area on a hillside, with each Gospel writer selecting and arranging material for his purpose. Others think Jesus taught the same themes more than once, as traveling teachers commonly did. Either explanation accounts for the differences without contradiction.

Matthew arranges Jesus’ teaching into five major blocks (chapters 5–7; 10; 13; 18; 24–25). Each ends with a similar closing formula: “when Jesus had ended these sayings” (7:28; compare 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). The Sermon on the Mount is the first and best known.

2.brief: Jesus opens His mouth and begins to teach them. The King who has announced the kingdom now describes the life of those who belong to it.
2.explain:
“Then He opened His mouth”

The expression is a Hebrew way of introducing solemn or significant speech (Job 3:1; Acts 8:35; 10:34). It may sound unnecessary in English, but it tells the reader to pay attention: what follows is important.

“and taught them, saying:”

“Them” refers to the disciples of 5:1. Teaching is one of the three activities Matthew uses to summarize Jesus’ ministry, alongside preaching the gospel of the kingdom and healing (4:23; 9:35). Preaching announced that the kingdom had come near (4:17). Teaching now explains what life in that kingdom looks like.
2.notes: The Greek verb is in the imperfect tense, which can describe ongoing or continuing action: He began teaching them or He was teaching them. It fits the length and range of the discourse that follows.

3.brief: Jesus declares, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Those who acknowledge their spiritual need and depend on God receive the kingdom as a gift.
3.explain:
“Blessed”

The Greek word makarios describes the condition of someone who has God’s favor and is truly well in His sight. “Happy” is too thin a translation, because the blessing does not depend on circumstances or feelings. The Old Testament uses the same kind of declaration: “Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly” (Psalm 1:1); “Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven” (Psalm 32:1).

The Beatitudes are declarations, not commands. Jesus does not say, Make yourselves poor in spirit. He announces who is blessed and why. These statements describe the character of those who belong to the kingdom and the blessing God gives them. They are not steps for earning entrance. They describe what the King produces in His people.

“are the poor in spirit,”

The word for “poor” (ptōchos) describes someone destitute, a beggar with nothing to offer. “In spirit” moves the meaning from economic condition to inward condition. The poor in spirit are those who know they have no spiritual resources of their own with which to stand before God.

This builds on a familiar Old Testament theme. The “poor” were often the humble godly who depended on the LORD because they had nowhere else to turn (Psalm 34:6). God says, “On this one will I look: On him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, And who trembles at My word” (Isaiah 66:2). Poverty of spirit is not low self-esteem or a timid personality. It is an honest view of oneself before God, like the tax collector who could only pray, “God, be merciful to me a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

“For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

The promise is stated in the present tense: the kingdom is theirs. “The kingdom of heaven” means the reign of God, which Jesus announced as having come near (4:17). The kingdom belongs to those who know they cannot earn it. It is received as a gift. God’s reign is already present through Jesus and will come in its fullness when He returns.
3.notes:
Matthew uses this phrase more than thirty times, where Mark and Luke usually say “the kingdom of God.” Many Jews of the period reverently used “heaven” in place of God’s name (compare Daniel 4:26, “Heaven rules”). The two expressions mean the same thing, as Matthew 19:23–24 shows by using both in successive verses.

Luke 6:20 reads “Blessed are you poor.” Matthew includes “in spirit.” The difference concerns the wording of the blessing.

4.brief: Those who mourn are blessed, “For they shall be comforted.” Jesus promises God’s comfort to those who grieve over sin and the brokenness of the world.
4.explain:
“Blessed are those who mourn,”

The Greek word pentheō is a strong word for grief, often used for mourning the dead (Mark 16:10). Following the first Beatitude, the mourning here most naturally includes grief over sin: our own sin, the sin of God’s people, and the damage sin has done in the world. It also includes the sorrow of God’s people who suffer under evil and wait for Him to make things right. Isaiah 61, echoed in these verses, speaks of those “who mourn in Zion” (Isaiah 61:3).

Not every sorrow is blessed. Paul distinguishes “godly sorrow,” which leads to repentance and salvation, from “the sorrow of the world,” which produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). The mourning Jesus blesses turns toward God rather than away from Him.

“For they shall be comforted.”

The passive voice points to God as the One who comforts. His comfort begins now, as the God of all comfort meets His people in their troubles (2 Corinthians 1:3–4), and it will be complete when “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). Israel had long waited for the comfort God promised (Isaiah 40:1), and devout people like Simeon were “waiting for the Consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25). With Jesus, that promised comfort has arrived.
4.notes: Several Beatitudes use passive verbs without naming who acts: “shall be comforted,” “shall be filled,” “shall obtain mercy,” “shall be called sons of God.” Jewish speech often used this form out of reverence, leaving God unnamed as the obvious actor.

5.brief: The meek are blessed, “For they shall inherit the earth.” Meekness is strength yielded to God, and those who trust Him rather than grasp for control will receive the inheritance He promises.
5.explain:
“Blessed are the meek,”

The Greek word praus describes gentleness and humility, a strength that is under control. It does not mean weakness. Moses, one of the strongest leaders in Scripture, is described as “very humble, more than all men who were on the face of the earth” (Numbers 12:3), where the Greek Old Testament uses this word. Jesus applies the same word to Himself: “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (11:29), and He enters Jerusalem “lowly, and sitting on a donkey” (21:5).

Meekness toward God means submitting to His will and trusting Him rather than fighting for our own way. Meekness toward people means gentleness, especially when wronged. It prepares for Jesus’ teaching on non-retaliation later in this chapter (5:39–42).

“For they shall inherit the earth.”

Jesus is quoting Psalm 37:11: “But the meek shall inherit the earth.” In that psalm, the meek are those who do not fret over the success of evildoers but rest in the LORD and wait for Him (Psalm 37:1, 7). The Hebrew word can mean “land” or “earth.” In the psalm, it refers to the promised land. On Jesus’ lips the promise reaches to the whole earth, which will be fully given to God’s people in the new heavens and new earth (Revelation 5:10; 21:1). An inheritance is received, not seized.
5.notes:
Psalm 37 repeats the promise of inheriting the land in 5:9, 11, 22, 29, and 34. Matthew 5:5 closely resembles Psalm 37:11.

The adjective praus can mean gentle or meek. Its use for a tamed animal in some Greek writing illustrates gentleness, but does not by itself define every use of the word.

6.brief: Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, “For they shall be filled.” People who long both for right standing with God and for lives conformed to His will find that longing satisfied by Him.
6.explain:
“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst”

Jesus uses the most basic human needs to picture spiritual longing. In a land where many knew real hunger and where water was precious, this language describes desperate need, not a mild appetite. The psalmists used the same picture: “My soul thirsts for You; My flesh longs for You In a dry and thirsty land Where there is no water” (Psalm 63:1; compare Psalm 42:1–2). The Greek participles describe an ongoing desire.

“for righteousness,”

In Matthew, “righteousness” means a life that is right with God and conforms to His will (3:15; 5:10, 20; 6:1, 33). It includes the longing to be right with God, the longing to live rightly before Him, and the longing to see His right order established in the world. Matthew’s emphasis falls on doing the will of God (5:20; 7:21), but the Sermon makes clear that this righteousness flows from God and is something He gives to those who long for it.

“For they shall be filled.”

The verb chortazō means to be fed until fully satisfied. Matthew uses it when the crowds “all ate and were filled” at the feeding of the five thousand (14:20). God is the One who fills. The satisfaction begins now and will be complete when His kingdom fully comes.
6.notes:
The Greek noun dikaiosynē can refer to righteousness or justice. It occurs in Matthew 3:15; 5:6, 10, 20; 6:1, 33; and 21:32.

Luke records, “Blessed are you who hunger now, For you shall be filled” (Luke 6:21), emphasizing the physical need of Jesus’ poor followers. Matthew’s “for righteousness” draws out the spiritual dimension.

7.brief: The merciful are blessed, “For they shall obtain mercy.” Those who turn compassion into action toward others show that they have received God’s mercy and will receive it fully.
7.explain:
“Blessed are the merciful,”

Mercy is compassion that acts. It shows kindness to those who are hurting and forgiveness to those who are guilty. Jesus twice quotes God’s word through Hosea, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (9:13; 12:7; Hosea 6:6), against religious leaders who valued ritual correctness over compassion. In Matthew, people in need repeatedly cry out to Jesus, “Have mercy on us” (9:27; 15:22; 20:30), and He responds.

“For they shall obtain mercy.”

The merciful will receive mercy from God, both now and at the final judgment. This does not mean mercy is earned by being merciful. Mercy received produces mercy given. Jesus’ parable of the unforgiving servant makes the point clearly: the servant who had been forgiven an enormous debt refused to forgive a small one and showed that God’s mercy had not changed his heart (18:21–35). The master asks, “Should you not also have had compassion on your fellow servant, just as I had pity on you?” (18:33).
7.notes:
Matthew 5:3–10 contain eight blessings, and 5:11 adds a ninth addressed directly to the disciples. “Righteousness” ends both 5:6 and 5:10, dividing the first eight into two groups of four.

The words “compassion” and “pity” in Matthew 18:33 translate the same Greek verb (eleeō) that stands behind “merciful” and “obtain mercy” here.

8.brief: The pure in heart are blessed, “For they shall see God.” A heart with undivided affection for God is promised the highest blessing of all, seeing Him.
8.explain:
“Blessed are the pure in heart,”

The Greek word katharos means clean, free from impurity, unmixed. The “heart” in Scripture is the center of a person’s thoughts, desires, and will. To be pure in heart is to be inwardly clean and single in devotion to God, without hidden motives or divided loyalties.

This stands against the religious emphasis on outward ritual purity. Jesus later rebukes scribes and Pharisees for cleaning “the outside of the cup and dish” while leaving the inside full of greed and self-indulgence (23:25–26). He teaches that evil comes from the heart (15:18–19). The psalmist asks, “Who may ascend into the hill of the LORD?” and answers, “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). Purity of heart is not something a person produces alone. David prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).

“For they shall see God.”

This is the highest blessing Scripture holds out. God told Moses, “You cannot see My face; for no man shall see Me, and live” (Exodus 33:20). Yet the promise stands: God’s servants “shall see His face” (Revelation 22:4), and “we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2). In this life, believers already see God in a real though partial way, perceiving Him by faith and beholding “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6; John 14:9). The full vision of God awaits the age to come.

9.brief: The peacemakers are blessed, “For they shall be called sons of God.” Those who work to restore peace reflect the character of their Father and are recognized as His children.
9.explain:
“Blessed are the peacemakers,”

Peacemakers are not simply peaceful people or people who avoid conflict. They actively make peace where there is division. Behind the word stands the Hebrew idea of shalom: wholeness, right relationships, and well-being. Peacemaking includes reconciling people to God, the ministry of reconciliation Paul describes (2 Corinthians 5:18–20), and reconciling people to one another, which Jesus will address in 5:23–24.

True peace rests on truth and righteousness. “The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3:18). Jesus also warns that His coming will divide even households (10:34–36). Peacemaking therefore does not mean peace at any price or the silencing of truth to avoid discomfort.

“For they shall be called sons of God.”

God Himself will call them His sons, acknowledging them as His own. In Hebrew idiom, being a “son” of something means sharing its character (compare “son of peace,” Luke 10:6). Peacemakers show the family likeness of “the God of peace” (Romans 15:33; Hebrews 13:20), who made peace with sinners “through the blood of His cross” (Colossians 1:20). “Sons” here includes all believers, women and men, who are “sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:26) and so share in the inheritance. Jesus returns to this theme in 5:45, where loving enemies shows that disciples are “sons of your Father in heaven.”
9.notes: The Greek eirēnopoios appears only here in the New Testament. Its related verb appears in Colossians 1:20, “having made peace through the blood of His cross.”

10.brief: Those persecuted for righteousness’ sake are blessed, “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” The list ends where it began, with the kingdom, showing that suffering for doing right does not cancel belonging to God’s reign.
10.explain:
“Blessed are those who are persecuted”

The life described in 5:3–9 will not always be welcomed. The verb means to pursue, harass, or hunt down. The Greek participle describes people who have been persecuted and continue to bear its effects.

“for righteousness’ sake,”

The cause matters. Jesus blesses those who suffer because they live according to God’s will, not those who suffer for wrongdoing, foolishness, or harshness. Peter makes the same distinction: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, a thief, an evildoer, or as a busybody in other people’s matters. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed” (1 Peter 4:15–16).

“For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

The promise repeats the promise of 5:3 word for word, again in the present tense. The two identical promises frame the Beatitudes, showing that all eight describe the same people. Those who suffer for the King’s righteousness already share in His kingdom.
10.notes:
Matthew 5:3 and 5:10 end with the same promise, enclosing the eight Beatitudes of 5:3–10 as a unit. Matthew 5:11 adds a ninth blessing, which applies the eighth directly to the disciples in the second person, and 5:12 continues it.

The Greek perfect participle (dediōgmenoi) describes a past action with continuing results: those who have been persecuted.

11.brief: Jesus turns directly to His disciples: they are blessed when people insult them, persecute them, and falsely say every kind of evil against them for His sake. Loyalty to Jesus will bring opposition, and that opposition marks them as His.
11.explain:
“Blessed are you”

Jesus shifts from “those who” to “you.” The blessing of 5:10 is now applied personally to the disciples sitting before Him.

“when they revile and persecute you,”

“Revile” means to insult, mock, or heap abuse on someone. Matthew uses the same verb at the cross, where even the robbers crucified with Jesus “reviled Him with the same thing” (27:44). “Persecute” repeats the verb of 5:10.

“and say all kinds of evil against you falsely”

Opposition will include slander. “Falsely” is an important qualification. The blessing applies when the accusations are untrue. It does not cover criticism a disciple has earned.

“for My sake.”

In 5:10, persecution was “for righteousness’ sake.” Now it is “for My sake.” Jesus places loyalty to Himself in the same position as loyalty to God’s righteousness. The prophets suffered for the sake of the LORD. Jesus asks His followers to suffer for His own sake, a claim that only makes sense if He stands where God stands.
11.notes: Luke records, “Blessed are you when men hate you, and when they exclude you, and revile you, and cast out your name as evil, For the Son of Man’s sake” (Luke 6:22), including social exclusion among the forms of persecution.

12.brief: He tells them to rejoice and be exceedingly glad, because their reward in heaven is great and the prophets before them were persecuted in the same way. Suffering for Christ places His disciples in the company of God’s faithful messengers and carries a sure reward.
12.explain:
“Rejoice and be exceedingly glad,”

Jesus gives two commands. The second describes exultant, overflowing joy. Rejoicing is not suggested as an option for the spiritually advanced. It is the fitting response because of what persecution for Jesus’ sake means.

“for great is your reward in heaven,”

The reward is kept with God, secure and certain, to be revealed when the Son of Man comes (16:27). Rewards in Matthew are not wages that earn salvation. They are God’s generous recognition of faithfulness (6:4, 6, 18; 10:42; 25:21).

“for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

The prophets suffered for speaking God’s word. Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15), and Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). Jesus later charges the religious leaders with being the sons of those who murdered the prophets (23:29–37). By saying “the prophets who were before you,” Jesus places His disciples in the same line.

13.brief: Jesus tells His disciples, “You are the salt of the earth,” and warns that salt which loses its flavor is good for nothing but to be thrown out. His people are to have a real, preserving influence in the world, and a disciple who loses that distinctiveness loses his usefulness.
13.explain:
“You are the salt of the earth;”

“You” is emphatic and plural. Jesus is speaking to the same people He has just described in the Beatitudes, including those who will be persecuted (5:10–12). He does not command them to become salt. He tells them what they already are.

Salt was essential in the ancient world. It preserved meat and fish from decay in a world without refrigeration, and it gave flavor to food (Job 6:6). “The earth” refers to the whole human world. Jesus’ disciples are to have a preserving and seasoning influence in a world inclined toward corruption.

“but if the salt loses its flavor,”

Much of the salt used in Israel came from the Dead Sea region and was mixed with other minerals. Moisture could dissolve the true salt and leave behind a residue that still looked like salt but had no saltiness. Pure sodium chloride does not lose its saltiness. The picture is of salt that has become mixed with so much else that it no longer does what salt is meant to do.

“how shall it be seasoned?”

Once salt has lost its saltiness, nothing can restore it. The question has no answer, and that is the point.

“It is then good for nothing but to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men.”

Useless salt was thrown onto paths, where people walked over it. The warning follows directly after the promise of persecution (5:10–12). The pressure to avoid opposition by blending in with the world is the very pressure that would make a disciple lose his distinctiveness, and with it his usefulness to God.
13.notes: The Greek verb mōrainō normally means to become foolish and is related to the word “fool” in 5:22. The underlying Hebrew may have been a word that means both “tasteless” and “foolish.” Paul uses the same Greek verb when he says God has “made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Corinthians 1:20).

14.brief: Jesus declares, “You are the light of the world,” like a city on a hill that cannot be hidden. The life of His people is meant to be seen.
14.explain:
“You are the light of the world.”

Again “you” is emphatic. Israel had been called to be “a light to the Gentiles” (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Matthew has just quoted Isaiah’s promise fulfilled in Jesus’ ministry in Galilee: “The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light” (4:16). Jesus is the light (John 8:12). His disciples become light because they have received His light and now reflect it.

“The world” reaches beyond Israel to all peoples. Already in the Sermon, Jesus is pointing toward the mission He will give at the end of the Gospel to “make disciples of all the nations” (28:19).

“A city that is set on a hill cannot be hidden.”

Towns in Galilee were often built on hilltops, visible for miles by day and by their lamps at night. Jerusalem itself stood on Mount Zion, and the prophets foresaw the nations streaming to “the mountain of the LORD’s house” (Isaiah 2:2–3). Jesus is not telling His disciples to try to be seen. A city on a hill is seen because of where it stands. The people of the kingdom will be visible by the nature of the life God has given them.

15.brief: No one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket; it goes on a lampstand to give light to everyone in the house. Hiding the light defeats the very reason it was lit.
15.explain:
“Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a basket,”

The lamp was a small clay vessel filled with olive oil, a common item in every home. The “basket” was a container used to measure grain. Placing it over a lamp would hide the light and serve no purpose. No one would go to the trouble of lighting a lamp only to cover it.

“but on a lampstand,”

The lamp was set on a stand or ledge where its light could spread.

“and it gives light to all who are in the house.”

Most ordinary homes in Galilee had a single main room. One lamp, properly placed, gave light to the whole household. The disciple’s light begins with those nearest to him.
15.notes: The Greek modios was a measuring container holding a little over two gallons of dry goods (about 8.75 liters).

16.brief: Jesus commands, “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.” Disciples’ visible good works are meant to turn attention and praise toward the Father, not themselves.
16.explain:
“Let your light so shine before men,”

“So” means “in this way,” like the lamp set on its stand. Jesus does not command the disciples to produce light but to let it shine, to stop hiding what God has given.

“that they may see your good works”

The light is expressed in conduct, not only in words. “Good works” describes deeds that are good and attractive, the kind of goodness others can recognize. The character described in the Beatitudes becomes visible in mercy, peacemaking, purity, and faithfulness.

“and glorify your Father in heaven.”

The goal is that people give glory to God, not to the disciples. This is the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls God the disciples’ “Father.” Their good works are the visible life of children who reflect their Father, and they lead others to honor Him.
16.notes:
In 6:1 Jesus warns, “Take heed that you do not do your charitable deeds before men, to be seen by them.” The two commands do not conflict. The difference lies in the motive. In 5:16 the purpose is the Father’s glory. In 6:1 the purpose is to be admired by others.

This is the first of seventeen occurrences of “Father” in the Sermon on the Mount.

17.brief: Jesus says, “Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to destroy but to fulfill.” He brings Scripture to its intended completion through His person, His perfect obedience, His saving work, and His authoritative teaching.
17.explain:
“Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets.”

Jesus anticipates a misunderstanding. His authority, His fresh teaching, and His conflicts with religious leaders could lead people to think He was setting aside the Scriptures. “Destroy” means to tear down, abolish, or annul. Matthew uses the same verb for the destruction of the temple (24:2; 26:61). “The Law or the Prophets” is a common way of referring to the Hebrew Scriptures as a whole (7:12; 22:40).

The words “I came” imply that Jesus has come from somewhere with a mission. He speaks this way several times in Matthew (9:13; 10:34–35; 20:28).

“I did not come to destroy but to fulfill.”

“Fulfill” is one of Matthew’s key words. He has already used it repeatedly for Scripture coming to pass in Jesus’ life (1:22; 2:15, 17, 23; 4:14). Jesus fulfills the Law and the Prophets by bringing them to their intended goal. His teaching reveals the full meaning of the law’s commands, as the rest of this chapter will show (5:21–48). His life obeys the law perfectly (3:15). His death and resurrection accomplish what its sacrifices, promises, and prophecies pointed toward (26:28; Hebrews 10:1–14).

Because Jesus fulfills the law, some parts of it now function differently. The sacrifices are completed in His once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:11–14), and the food laws pointed toward a cleansing that comes from within (Mark 7:19). These are fulfilled, not discarded. The moral will of God revealed in the law remains and is deepened in Jesus’ teaching.
17.notes:
Interpreters have understood “fulfill” in several ways: Jesus confirms and upholds the law; Jesus fills up its meaning through His teaching; or Jesus brings the law to completion in His person and work. Matthew’s consistent use of the verb for prophecy coming to pass favors the third view, which includes the other two.

The Jewish Scriptures were often described in two parts (the Law and the Prophets) or three (the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms or Writings, Luke 24:44). Either way, the phrase refers to the entire Old Testament.

18.brief: Jesus solemnly affirms that until heaven and earth pass away, not the smallest letter or stroke will pass from the law until all is fulfilled. God’s Word stands firm in every detail and will accomplish all it was given to do.
18.explain:
“For assuredly, I say to you,”

“Assuredly” translates the Hebrew word amen. Others used “Amen” to agree with something already said. Jesus uses it at the beginning of His own statements, a way of speaking found only on His lips. It signals solemn authority and appears more than thirty times in Matthew.

“till heaven and earth pass away,”

Heaven and earth are the most lasting things people know. The expression means as long as the present creation endures. Later Jesus says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away” (24:35), placing His own words alongside the law in their permanence.

“one jot or one tittle”

The “jot” is the yod, the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The “tittle” is a tiny stroke or hook that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another similar letter. Jesus is speaking of the smallest details of the written law.

“will by no means pass from the law”

The Greek uses an emphatic double negative: it will certainly not pass away.

“till all is fulfilled.”

This is a different verb from “fulfill” in 5:17. It means until everything happens or until all is accomplished. Everything the law requires, foreshadows, and promises will come to pass. Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection accomplish much of it, and the end of the age will complete it.
18.notes:
The verse contains two time limits: “till heaven and earth pass away” and “till all is fulfilled.” Both stress that God’s Word will remain in force until its purposes are fully accomplished.

“And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tittle of the law to fail” (Luke 16:17).

19.brief: Whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom, but whoever does and teaches them will be called great. Jesus’ followers are to do and teach God’s commands as Jesus has fulfilled them, treating none of them carelessly in life or in teaching.
19.explain:
“Whoever therefore breaks one of the least of these commandments,”

“Therefore” builds on 5:18: since every detail of the law stands, no part may be treated lightly. “Breaks” means to loosen, relax, or set aside, and it shares a root with “destroy” in 5:17. Jewish teachers sometimes classified commandments as “light” or “heavy.” Jesus warns against treating the “least” commandments as optional.

“These commandments” refers to the law as Jesus interprets and fulfills it. In the verses that follow, He will show what the commandments truly require.

“and teaches men so,”

Teachers carry greater responsibility because they influence others (James 3:1). Setting aside a commandment privately is serious. Teaching others to do the same multiplies the harm.

“shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven;”

Jesus elsewhere speaks of differing greatness in the kingdom (11:11; 18:4). This verse concerns standing and greatness within the kingdom, and 5:20 turns to the question of entrance. Jesus offers no comfort here to anyone who makes a practice of setting aside God’s commands and teaching others to do the same.

“but whoever does and teaches them, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

Doing comes before teaching. Greatness in God’s kingdom belongs to those who obey God’s Word and faithfully teach others to obey it.
19.notes:
Later Jewish sources discuss which commandments were weightier and which were lighter, sometimes contrasting the command about a bird’s nest (Deuteronomy 22:6–7) with honoring parents (Deuteronomy 5:16). Jesus Himself speaks of “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith” (23:23), yet He adds that the lesser things should not be left undone.

Interpreters differ over whether “these commandments” refers directly to the Mosaic commands or to Jesus’ teaching that follows. The relationship between the two is discussed in 5:17–20.

20.brief: Jesus warns that unless His disciples’ righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven. This is more serious than being called least in the kingdom: righteousness that is merely outward does not enter at all, so Jesus requires a righteousness that reaches the heart and governs conduct.
20.explain:
“For I say to you,”

Jesus speaks with His own authority, preparing for the six statements that follow, each introduced with “But I say to you.”

“that unless your righteousness exceeds”

“Exceeds” means to overflow or go far beyond. Jesus is not asking for slightly more of the same thing.

“the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees,”

The scribes were experts in the law and its teachers. The Pharisees were a devout movement known for strict observance of the law and its traditions, including tithing, Sabbath keeping, and ritual purity. In the eyes of ordinary people, they were the most righteous people in Israel. Their righteousness, however, was largely external and concerned with being seen by others (6:1–18; 23:5, 23–28).

“you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven.”

The statement would have shocked Jesus’ hearers. If the most religious people in the nation fell short, who could enter? The greater righteousness Jesus requires is not more rule-keeping. It is different in kind: righteousness of the heart that reaches anger, desire, words, and love for enemies, as 5:21–48 will show.

The Sermon has already shown where such righteousness begins. The kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit (5:3), and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled (5:6). The righteousness God requires is the righteousness He supplies, through forgiveness in Jesus’ blood (26:28) and through the new heart He promised to give by His Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26–27).
20.notes:
Josephus reports more than six thousand Pharisees in Herod’s time (Antiquities 17.42). They were a recognized Jewish religious movement, distinct from the Sadducees.

Matthew 5:20 states the theme. The six contrasts that follow (5:21–47) illustrate the greater righteousness, and 5:48 sums it up.

21.brief: Jesus recalls the command given long ago, “You shall not murder,” and the judgment that follows murder. He begins to show how His teaching brings the command to its full depth.
21.explain:
“You have heard that it was said to those of old,”

Most people in Jesus’ day did not own copies of the Scriptures. They heard the law read and explained in the synagogue. “Those of old” refers to earlier generations, beginning with Israel at Sinai. This formula introduces each of the six contrasts in 5:21–47.

Jesus is not contradicting Moses. He has just declared that He came to fulfill the law (5:17). He contrasts the law as it had commonly been heard and taught with its full meaning as He reveals it. Some of the statements He quotes are Scripture word for word (5:27). Others combine Scripture with a popular interpretation (5:43).

“You shall not murder,”

This is the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17). The Hebrew word refers to the unlawful killing of a human being, not every form of taking life.

“and whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.”

This line is not a direct quotation but a summary of the law’s provisions for murder (Exodus 21:12; Numbers 35:12). “The judgment” refers to the local court that heard such cases (Deuteronomy 16:18). As commonly taught, the commandment concerned the act of murder and its legal consequence.
21.notes:
The formula You have heard that it was said … But I say to you appears with variations in 5:21–22, 27–28, 31–32, 33–34, 38–39, and 43–44. These contrasts are sometimes called the “antitheses.”

The Greek could also be translated by those of old. The NKJV’s “to those of old” fits the reference to what was spoken to Israel at Sinai.

22.brief: Jesus says that anyone angry with his brother without a cause faces judgment, and that contemptuous words like “Raca!” and “You fool!” bring greater danger, even of hell fire. The command against murder reaches the anger and contempt in the heart and on the tongue.
22.explain:
“But I say to you”

The prophets said, Thus says the LORD. Jesus says, “I say to you.” He speaks as the One who has the authority to declare the meaning of God’s law.

“that whoever is angry with his brother without a cause”

“Brother” refers first to a fellow member of God’s people, though the principle reaches to every person. Jesus is speaking of anger directed against a brother, the kind of resentment that, when it is nursed, grows into contempt and worse. Not all anger is sinful. Jesus Himself looked on His opponents “with anger, being grieved by the hardness of their hearts” (Mark 3:5), and Paul writes, “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). The NKJV’s “without a cause” identifies the anger Jesus condemns: resentful, unjustified anger toward another person.

“shall be in danger of the judgment.”

These are the same words used of the murderer in 5:21. The angry person stands where the murderer stood. Anger is the root from which murder grows (1 John 3:15).

“And whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!”

“Raca” is an Aramaic insult meaning something like “empty-head” or “worthless.” It expresses contempt.

“shall be in danger of the council.”

“The council” is the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court in Jerusalem.

“But whoever says, ‘You fool!”

“Fool” in biblical usage often describes a person who is morally worthless or godless: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1). To call someone a fool in this way is to write him off.

“shall be in danger of hell fire.”

“Hell” translates Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem. During Israel’s apostasy, children were sacrificed there to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), and the valley became a picture of God’s final judgment. The movement from local court to supreme court to hell fire is not a precise scale of penalties. It shows that human courts cannot judge anger and contempt, but God does.
22.notes:
The Greek word eikē is found in most manuscripts and is followed by the NKJV. Several of the oldest manuscripts do not include it. Either way, Scripture elsewhere shows that anger in itself is not always sinful (Mark 3:5; Ephesians 4:26).

Jesus calls the scribes and Pharisees “Fools and blind!” (23:17). His rebuke was a prophetic judgment on spiritual blindness, spoken by the One who will judge all people. Matthew 5:22 forbids the contempt that grows out of personal anger and treats another person as worthless.

23.brief: If someone is offering his gift at the altar and remembers that his brother has something against him, Jesus gives specific direction. Worship cannot ignore a broken relationship.
23.explain:
“Therefore”

Since anger and contempt are this serious before God (5:22), a disciple must deal with broken relationships urgently.

“if you bring your gift to the altar,”

Jesus pictures a worshiper at the temple in Jerusalem, bringing an offering to the priest at the altar. This is a moment of worship and devotion.

“and there remember”

The memory comes at the altar, in the act of worship.

“that your brother has something against you,”

Jesus does not say, if you have something against your brother. He says, if your brother has something against you. The worshiper is the one who has caused offense, or at least the one his brother believes has wronged him. Jesus places the responsibility to act on the one who caused the offense. Elsewhere He addresses the other side: “Whenever you stand praying, if you have anything against anyone, forgive him” (Mark 11:25).
23.notes: In Jewish teaching, certain wrongs against others required restitution before an offering could be made (Leviticus 6:1–7; Numbers 5:5–8). Jesus extends the principle from material wrongs to broken relationships.

24.brief: He is to leave the gift before the altar, go and be reconciled to his brother first, and then come and offer it. Seeking to make things right with others is so important to God that it comes before completing an act of worship.
24.explain:
“leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way.”

Jesus tells the worshiper to stop in the middle of a holy act. Offering a sacrifice was a sacred duty, yet it must wait.

“First be reconciled to your brother,”

“First” establishes the priority. To be reconciled means to move from hostility to restored relationship. The worshiper cannot control his brother’s response, but he must do his part. Paul writes, “If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men” (Romans 12:18).

“and then come and offer your gift.”

Worship is not canceled. God still wants the gift. Reconciliation restores worship to its proper place. Throughout Scripture, God refuses worship that is offered while His people ignore what He cares about most (1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11–17; Hosea 6:6).
24.notes:
Jesus is speaking in Galilee, roughly three days’ journey from the temple in Jerusalem. Leaving an offering at the altar to go home and seek reconciliation would have been startling. The vivid picture underlines how urgent the matter is.

The Greek verb used here (diallassomai) appears only here in the New Testament. Paul uses a related verb for reconciliation with God and with a spouse (Romans 5:10; 1 Corinthians 7:11; 2 Corinthians 5:18–20).

25.brief: Jesus urges settling quickly with an adversary while still on the way, before he hands you to the judge, the officer, and prison. Delay in making things right can lead to consequences that can no longer be avoided.
25.explain:
“Agree with your adversary quickly,”

“Agree” means to come to terms with, to be on good terms with. The “adversary” is an opponent in a lawsuit, possibly a creditor, since 5:26 speaks of payment. “Quickly” stresses urgency.

“while you are on the way with him,”

In the picture, the two parties are walking together to court. There is still time to settle.

“lest your adversary deliver you to the judge, the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison.”

The consequences follow one after another. Once the case reaches the judge, the matter is out of the defendant’s hands. The officer carries out the sentence, and prison follows. Imprisonment for debt was practiced in the Roman world (compare 18:30).

The picture comes from everyday legal life, but its placement after 5:22–24 suggests a deeper warning. Everyone is on the way to the judgment of God. Unresolved wrongs carry consequences that grow the longer they are left.
25.notes: Luke places a similar saying in the context of discerning the time and being ready for coming judgment (Luke 12:54–59), which supports reading it as a warning that reaches beyond earthly courts.

26.brief: Jesus assures them that the one thrown into prison will not get out until he has paid the last penny. The warning presses the urgency of reconciliation before the time of reckoning comes.
26.explain:
“Assuredly, I say to you,”

The solemn “Amen” formula marks this as a serious warning (see 5:18).

“you will by no means get out of there”

The Greek uses an emphatic negative. There is no escape.

“till you have paid the last penny.”

The “penny” was the quadrans, the smallest Roman copper coin, worth one sixty-fourth of a denarius, which was a laborer’s daily wage. The debt must be paid to the last fraction. Within the illustration, the prisoner remains until everything is paid. The saying stresses the seriousness of unresolved conflict and, in its wider application, the certainty of judgment.
26.notes:
Mark explains that the poor widow’s two small coins together made a quadrans (Mark 12:42).

Some in church history used this verse to support the idea of purgatory, a place of temporary purification after death. The saying is an illustration drawn from civil law about urgency in reconciliation. It does not describe conditions after death.

27.brief: Jesus recalls the command, “You shall not commit adultery.” He turns now from anger to sexual faithfulness.
27.explain:
“You have heard that it was said to those of old,”

Jesus uses the same formula as in 5:21.

“You shall not commit adultery.”

This is the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14; Deuteronomy 5:18). Adultery is sexual intercourse in which at least one partner is married to someone else. Under the law it was a capital offense (Leviticus 20:10), because it violated the marriage bond and threatened the family at the heart of Israel’s life. As the commandment was commonly taught, a man who had not committed the physical act could consider himself innocent.
27.notes: These words are found in the later manuscripts followed by the NKJV but are missing from several of the oldest. The phrase does not change the meaning, since the formula is used in full in 5:21 and 5:33.

28.brief: Jesus says that whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Faithfulness to God’s command reaches the desires a person cultivates, not only outward acts.
28.explain:
“But I say to you that whoever looks at a woman”

Jesus is not condemning a passing glance or the simple act of noticing that someone is attractive. The issue is the purpose behind the look, as the next phrase makes clear.

“to lust for her”

The Greek says in order to desire her. The look has a purpose: to possess her in the imagination. The verb for “lust” is the same verb the Greek Old Testament uses in the tenth commandment: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:17). Jesus joins the seventh and tenth commandments, showing that God’s law always reached the heart. The law itself forbade coveting another man’s wife, so Jesus is revealing what the law already intended. The principle applies equally to women.

“has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The heart is where adultery begins, and God sees the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). This does not mean that lust is as damaging to others as the physical act, or that a person who has lusted might as well commit the act. It means both stand guilty before God. Job understood this: “I have made a covenant with my eyes; Why then should I look upon a young woman?” (Job 31:1).
28.notes:
In the Greek Old Testament, Exodus 20:17 uses epithymeō (“covet,” “desire”), the same verb Jesus uses here. The word can describe good desire (Luke 22:15), but here it describes desire for what belongs to another.

The Greek word can mean “woman” or “wife.” Given the connection to the tenth commandment, Jesus may have another man’s wife primarily in view, but the principle extends to all lustful looking.

29.brief: If the right eye causes sin, it should be plucked out and thrown away, since losing one part is better than having the whole body cast into hell. With deliberately shocking language Jesus demands decisive action to remove whatever leads into sin, not bodily mutilation.
29.explain:
“If your right eye causes you to sin,”

The right side was regarded as the more important and valuable. “Causes you to sin” comes from a word picturing a trap or snare that trips someone up. The eye connects directly to the lustful look of 5:28.

“pluck it out and cast it from you;”

Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration to make His point. He is not commanding physical self-harm. Removing one eye would not stop lust, since lust comes from the heart (5:28; 15:19), and the left eye would remain. His words call for decisive, costly action against whatever leads a person into sin.

“for it is more profitable for you that one of your members perish, than for your whole body to be cast into hell.”

Jesus weighs loss against loss. Giving up something valuable now is better than losing everything in final judgment. “Hell” is again Gehenna (see 5:22). Jesus speaks plainly about the reality of judgment because sin is that serious.
29.notes:
The verb skandalizō is related to skandalon, originally the trigger of a trap. It describes something that trips a person and brings about his fall.

Jesus often used exaggeration to make a point memorable: a camel through a needle’s eye (19:24), a plank in the eye (7:3), straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel (23:24). The literal reading of 5:29–30 has been consistently rejected in Christian teaching.

30.brief: If the right hand causes sin, it should be cut off and thrown away for the same reason. The repetition reinforces how seriously disciples must deal with every occasion of sin, relying on the Spirit’s power to do so.
30.explain:
“And if your right hand causes you to sin,”

The hand represents what a person does: what he touches, takes, and pursues. The right hand was the stronger and more skillful hand, used for work and for making oaths.

“cut it off and cast it from you;”

Again Jesus uses exaggeration to call for decisive action, not physical injury.

“for it is more profitable for you that one of your members perish, than for your whole body to be cast into hell.”

Jesus repeats the conclusion of 5:29 word for word. The repetition reinforces the seriousness of the warning.
30.notes: Jesus repeats this teaching in 18:8–9, adding the foot, in the context of warnings against causing others to stumble. Mark 9:43–48 adds the description of hell as the place “where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched.”

31.brief: Jesus recalls the teaching that a man divorcing his wife should give her a certificate of divorce. That provision regulated divorce but had become a way to treat dismissal as a mere formality.
31.explain:
“Furthermore it has been said,”

The introduction is shorter than in 5:21 and 5:27, linking this teaching closely to the previous one on adultery.

“Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.”

This summarizes Deuteronomy 24:1–4. Moses did not command divorce. He regulated a practice that already existed. The law required a written certificate, which protected the woman by showing she had been legally released and was free to remarry. It also forbade a man from taking back a wife he had divorced after she married another man.

By Jesus’ day, the certificate had become the focus. As long as the paperwork was done, divorce was treated as acceptable. Jewish teachers debated the meaning of “some uncleanness” in Deuteronomy 24:1. Some held that divorce was allowed only for sexual immorality. Others allowed divorce for almost any reason a husband found displeasing. The Pharisees later tested Jesus on this very question: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for just any reason?” (19:3).
31.notes:
The Mishnah records that the school of Shammai permitted divorce only for unchastity, while the school of Hillel permitted it even if a wife spoiled a meal (Gittin 9:10).

Jesus later explains that “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so” (19:8).

In Jewish practice of the time, a husband could divorce his wife, but a wife generally could not initiate divorce. Women were therefore especially vulnerable to easy divorce.

32.brief: Jesus says that whoever divorces his wife for any reason except sexual immorality causes her to commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. He confronts faithless divorce as a serious wrong against the marriage God joined, naming sexual immorality as the exception here; Matthew 19 gives His fuller teaching.
32.explain:
“But I say to you that whoever divorces his wife for any reason except sexual immorality”

“Sexual immorality” translates porneia, a broad word for sexual sin. Here it refers to sexual unfaithfulness within the marriage. Sexual unfaithfulness is a grave violation of the marriage covenant and provides grounds for divorce, though Jesus does not require the innocent spouse to pursue it. Where a marriage ends on these grounds, the innocent spouse is free to remarry. In 19:4–9, Jesus grounds His teaching in God’s design at creation: “What God has joined together, let not man separate.”

“causes her to commit adultery;”

In that culture, a divorced woman usually needed to remarry for support and protection. A husband who divorced his wife without proper grounds pushed her toward a second marriage that God would regard as adulterous, because the first marriage had not been rightly ended in His sight. Jesus places the responsibility squarely on the husband who sends her away.

“and whoever marries a woman who is divorced commits adultery.”

In context, this refers to a woman divorced on grounds other than sexual immorality. The divorce actually ended the marriage, but ending it without grounds was sin. A remarriage that follows such a divorce violates the covenant that was wrongly broken, and Jesus calls it adultery. Matthew 19:3–9 gives His fuller teaching. The explanation of 19:9 addresses abandonment, abuse, repentance, and remarriage.

Jesus’ purpose is to uphold the permanence of marriage against easy divorce. His words are not meant to place divorced people beyond God’s grace. Paul later addresses a further situation, the abandonment of a believer by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). Many divorced believers were the wronged party, and for those who sinned, the gospel offers forgiveness and restoration.
32.notes:
Mark 10:11–12 and Luke 16:18 record Jesus’ teaching without the exception. Matthew, writing with Jewish readers in view, includes it in light of the debate over Deuteronomy 24:1.

Matthew uses porneia for the ground of divorce and a different word, moicheia, for adultery. Porneia is the broader term.

33.brief: Jesus recalls the command not to swear falsely but to perform one’s oaths to the Lord. He now addresses truthful speech.
33.explain:
“Again you have heard that it was said to those of old,”

The full formula of 5:21 returns, marking the beginning of the second group of three contrasts.

“You shall not swear falsely,”

An oath called on God as witness that a statement was true or that a promise would be kept. The law forbade swearing falsely by God’s name (Leviticus 19:12), which is closely related to the third commandment against taking His name in vain (Exodus 20:7).

“but shall perform your oaths to the Lord.”

The law required that vows made to God be kept (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23). The teaching was good as far as it went. The problem lay in how it was applied. Teachers distinguished between binding and non-binding oaths based on the wording used. An oath that did not mention God directly could be treated as less binding. Truthfulness had become a matter of technical formulas rather than honest speech. Jesus exposes this practice in 23:16–22, where swearing “by the temple” was considered non-binding but swearing “by the gold of the temple” was binding.
33.notes:
An oath affirmed the truth of a statement or the certainty of a promise by calling on God as witness. A vow was a promise made to God, often to give or do something. Both are in view here.

A whole tractate of the Mishnah (Shevuot, “Oaths”) discusses the conditions under which oaths were binding, showing how detailed these distinctions became.

34.brief: Jesus says, “do not swear at all,” neither by heaven, which is God’s throne. He targets oaths used to evade truthfulness, which sounded solemn while leaving room for escape, yet every such oath involves God.
34.explain:
“But I say to you, do not swear at all:”

In context, Jesus is addressing the everyday use of oaths to back up ordinary speech and the practice of using carefully chosen oaths to avoid being bound. Scripture elsewhere shows that a solemn oath is not sinful in itself. God swears by Himself (Hebrews 6:13). Paul calls God as his witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23). Jesus Himself answered when the high priest put Him under oath (26:63–64). Jesus is not forbidding a solemn oath in a court of law. He is forbidding the habit of propping up words with oaths, which suggests that unsworn words may not be true.

“neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne;”

People swore “by heaven” to avoid using God’s name directly, thinking such an oath was less binding. Jesus answers that heaven is God’s throne (Isaiah 66:1). Swearing by heaven still involves God.
34.notes:
Some Christian traditions, including many Anabaptists and Quakers, have understood this command as forbidding all oaths, including those in court. Most Christian traditions have understood it as forbidding casual and evasive oaths, based on the examples of God, Paul, and Jesus noted above.

“But above all, my brethren, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or with any other oath. But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (James 5:12).

35.brief: Nor should anyone swear by the earth, which is God’s footstool, or by Jerusalem, the city of the great King. Every substitute in an oath still belongs to God, so no oath escapes His notice.
35.explain:
“nor by the earth, for it is His footstool;”

Jesus continues to quote Isaiah 66:1: “Heaven is My throne, And earth is My footstool.” The earth belongs to God as surely as heaven does.

“nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.”

Jesus draws on Psalm 48:2, which calls Mount Zion “the city of the great King.” Jerusalem was holy because God had chosen it and placed His name there. Swearing by Jerusalem still invoked God.

36.brief: Nor should anyone swear by his own head, since he cannot make one hair white or black. Even a person’s own head is beyond his control, so swearing by it gives no real guarantee.
36.explain:
“Nor shall you swear by your head,”

Swearing by one’s head or life was a common way of staking oneself on a statement. It seemed to involve only the speaker.

“because you cannot make one hair white or black.”

No one can make his hair turn white with age or turn it back to its youthful color. A person does not truly control his own head. It belongs to God, so swearing by it still involves Him.
36.notes: Josephus reports that Herod the Great dyed his hair black to conceal his age (Antiquities 16.233).

37.brief: Jesus commands, “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No,’” for anything more comes from the evil one. His disciples are to be so consistently truthful that their plain word can be trusted without elaborate oaths.
37.explain:
“But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.”

A disciple’s words should be so reliable that oaths are unnecessary. A plain yes or no should be as trustworthy as any sworn statement.

“For whatever is more than these is from the evil one.”

The need for oaths arises in a world where lying is common. Adding oaths to ordinary speech reflects that world and plays into deception. The NKJV understands the phrase as referring to the devil, who is “a liar and the father of it” (John 8:44).
37.notes: The Greek phrase can be read as masculine (“the evil one”) or neuter (“evil”). The same ambiguity appears in 5:39 and in the Lord’s Prayer (6:13). In 13:19 and 13:38, Matthew clearly refers to the devil as “the wicked one.”

38.brief: Jesus recalls the principle, “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” That law limited punishment to fit the offense, but it was being used to justify personal revenge.
38.explain:
“You have heard that it was said,”

The shorter formula introduces the fifth contrast.

“An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.”

This principle appears three times in the law (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). It was given to judges, not to individuals (Deuteronomy 19:18–21). Its purpose was to ensure that punishment fit the crime and to restrain the human tendency to escalate revenge. In practice, it was often satisfied through payment of compensation rather than physical injury.

By Jesus’ day, a principle intended for courts had become a popular justification for personal revenge. The law itself had already forbidden this: “You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).
38.notes:
The principle is often called by its Latin name, lex talionis. A similar principle appears in the Code of Hammurabi. Later Jewish practice generally applied it through monetary compensation (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1).

Leviticus 19:18 both forbids personal vengeance and commands love for one’s neighbor. Jesus draws on this chapter again in 5:43, and its call to holiness (Leviticus 19:2) stands behind 5:48.

39.brief: Jesus tells His disciples not to resist an evil person, but to turn the other cheek to someone who slaps the right cheek. He calls them to let go of the urge to repay personal insult and humiliation; this does not require remaining exposed to physical violence.
39.explain:
“But I tell you not to resist an evil person.”

“Resist” here means to oppose in retaliation, to fight back in order to get even. In context, Jesus is addressing personal revenge, not every form of opposition to evil. The same Greek verb is used for resisting the devil (James 4:7) and for Paul’s opposing Peter to his face over the gospel (Galatians 2:11). Disciples are not to answer personal wrongs by striking back.

“But whoever slaps you on your right cheek,”

For a right-handed person, striking someone’s right cheek usually meant a backhanded slap. In that culture, such a blow was an insult more than an injury, an attack on a person’s honor.

“turn the other to him also.”

Rather than retaliate to defend his honor, the disciple is willing to bear further insult. Jesus did this at His trial when He was struck and spat upon (26:67), fulfilling Isaiah 50:6: “I gave My back to those who struck Me, And My cheeks to those who plucked out the beard.”

This command does not forbid governing authorities from restraining evil (Romans 13:1–4). It does not require victims of abuse to remain in danger. Paul protested unjust treatment and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25). The command addresses the personal response to insult and wrong: no retaliation, no revenge.
39.notes:
Later Jewish law imposed a fine for a slap on the cheek and doubled it for a backhanded blow, because it was the greater insult (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:6).

When an officer struck Jesus during His questioning before Annas, He answered, “If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike Me?” (John 18:22–23). Non-retaliation does not mean silence in the face of injustice.

40.brief: If someone sues to take the tunic, the disciple is to let him have the cloak as well. Jesus calls His followers to yield their own rights in love rather than fight to protect them.
40.explain:
“If anyone wants to sue you and take away your tunic,”

The setting is a lawsuit. The “tunic” was the inner garment worn next to the skin.

“let him have your cloak also.”

The “cloak” was the outer garment, which also served as a blanket at night. The law protected it. A creditor who took a cloak as a pledge had to return it by sunset, “for that is his only covering” (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:12–13). Jesus calls His disciples to be willing to give up even what the law guaranteed them, rather than fight to keep it.
40.notes: Luke 6:29 reverses the order, “from him who takes away your cloak, do not withhold your tunic either,” which seems to picture robbery rather than a lawsuit.

41.brief: If someone compels a disciple to go one mile, he is to go two. Even forced service becomes an opportunity to show willing, generous love.
41.explain:
“And whoever compels you to go one mile,”

“Compels” is a technical term for the right of Roman soldiers and officials to force civilians to carry their equipment or perform other services. Matthew uses the same verb when the soldiers “compelled” Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus’ cross (27:32). The Roman mile was a thousand paces, slightly shorter than a modern mile. This practice was a hated reminder of foreign occupation.

“go with him two.”

The soldier could require one mile. Jesus calls His disciples to go two. The first mile fulfills the obligation, and the second goes beyond what was demanded. This is the greater righteousness of the kingdom in action, the righteousness that “exceeds” (5:20) and does “more than others” (5:47). By going beyond what is required, the disciple turns an act of oppression into an act of freely given kindness, offered without resentment.
41.notes: The Greek angareuō comes from a Persian word for royal couriers who could press people and animals into service. It appears in the New Testament only here, in 27:32, and in the parallel Mark 15:21.

42.brief: Jesus commands giving to the one who asks and not turning away from someone who wants to borrow. A generous spirit replaces the instinct to hold on to what is one’s own.
42.explain:
“Give to him who asks you,”

Jesus calls for a generous disposition toward those in need. This does not require reckless giving that harms the giver’s family or enables destructive behavior. Scripture elsewhere calls for wisdom in giving and for providing first for one’s own household (2 Thessalonians 3:10; 1 Timothy 5:8). The point is a heart that is ready to give rather than looking for reasons not to.

“and from him who wants to borrow from you do not turn away.”

The law commanded Israel to lend freely to the poor, even when the year of release was near and the loan might never be repaid (Deuteronomy 15:7–11). Lending to a fellow Israelite in need was to be done without interest (Exodus 22:25). Jesus calls His disciples not to turn their backs on those who ask for help.

43.brief: Jesus recalls the saying, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” The law commanded love of neighbor, but hatred of enemies had been added to it.
43.explain:
“You have heard that it was said,”

The shorter formula introduces the sixth and final contrast.

“You shall love your neighbor”

This command comes from Leviticus 19:18. In its original setting, “neighbor” referred primarily to a fellow Israelite, but the same chapter extends love to the foreigner living among God’s people: “you shall love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34).

“and hate your enemy.”

No Old Testament text commands hatred of enemies. This was a popular inference: if “neighbor” meant fellow Israelite, then an enemy outside that circle could be hated. Some psalms express hatred toward God’s enemies (Psalm 139:21–22), and the Dead Sea community taught its members to hate the sons of darkness. Yet the law also commanded kindness toward an enemy: returning his straying ox or donkey and helping his burdened animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and giving him food and water when he was hungry and thirsty (Proverbs 25:21). Jesus corrects a teaching that had added to God’s Word.
43.notes: The Community Rule found at Qumran instructs members to love all the sons of light … and to hate all the sons of darkness (1QS 1:9–10).

44.brief: Jesus commands His disciples to love their enemies, bless those who curse them, do good to those who hate them, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute them. Love for enemies takes concrete form in blessing, good deeds, and prayer.
44.explain:
“But I say to you, love your enemies,”

The verb for love (agapaō) describes a love that seeks the good of another person. It is a matter of will and action rather than warm feeling. “Enemies” includes personal enemies and those who oppose God’s people: Roman soldiers, hostile neighbors, and persecutors.

“bless those who curse you,”

To bless is to speak good to someone and to ask God’s favor on him. When cursed, the disciple answers with blessing.

“do good to those who hate you,”

Love becomes concrete action.

“and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you,”

Prayer reaches deepest. “Spitefully use” means to mistreat, abuse, or insult. “Persecute” ties this command back to the Beatitudes (5:10–12). The disciple is to pray for the very people who cause him to suffer.
44.notes: The phrases “bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you” and “spitefully use you” are found in the majority of manuscripts and are included in the NKJV. Several of the oldest manuscripts have the shorter reading, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. The longer wording appears without question in Luke 6:27–28, so the teaching is clearly Jesus’ either way.

45.brief: By loving their enemies and praying for those who persecute them, disciples show that they are sons of their Father in heaven, who makes His sun rise and sends rain on the evil and the good alike. The Father’s generous kindness to all is the pattern for His children.
45.explain:
“that you may be sons of your Father in heaven;”

Loving enemies does not earn a place in God’s family. It shows that a person belongs there. As in 5:9, being a “son” means bearing the family likeness. Children who love their enemies resemble their Father.

“for He makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good,”

Jesus calls it “His sun.” The sun belongs to God, and He causes it to rise every day on those who love Him and those who reject Him.

“and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.”

In an agricultural land like Israel, rain meant life. God does not withhold rain from the fields of those who hate Him. His daily kindness reaches everyone.
45.notes: “For He is kind to the unthankful and evil” (Luke 6:35).

46.brief: If disciples love only those who love them, what reward will they have, since even tax collectors do the same? Loving those who love us back is ordinary human behavior, not the distinctive mark of God’s children.
46.explain:
“For if you love those who love you, what reward have you?”

Loving those who love us is natural. It requires no special grace and earns no special recognition from God. Jesus returns to the theme of reward (5:12; 6:1).

“Do not even the tax collectors do the same?”

Tax collectors were Jews who collected tolls and taxes for Rome or for Herod Antipas. They were known for overcharging and were regarded as traitors and sinners (9:10–11; 18:17). Yet even they loved their friends and families. Love that only returns love rises no higher than theirs.
46.notes: The Gospel writer himself was a tax collector when Jesus called him (9:9; 10:3). His Gospel alone identifies the apostle Matthew as “the tax collector” in the list of the Twelve.

47.brief: If disciples greet only their own brethren, they do nothing more than others, since even tax collectors do so. Kingdom love reaches past the circle of the familiar and friendly.
47.explain:
“And if you greet your brethren only,”

A greeting was more than a casual hello. It was a wish of peace, an act of recognition and welcome. “Brethren” refers to one’s own people or group.

“what do you do more than others?”

The word “more” echoes 5:20, where Jesus required righteousness that “exceeds” that of the scribes and Pharisees. The greater righteousness shows itself in love that reaches beyond one’s own circle.

“Do not even the tax collectors do so?”

Even those regarded as outsiders and sinners greet their own.
47.notes:
The NKJV follows the majority of manuscripts in reading “tax collectors” here. Several of the oldest manuscripts read “Gentiles,” which is followed by many modern translations.

The Greek word perisson is related to the verb translated “exceeds” in 5:20.

48.brief: Jesus concludes, “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” He calls His disciples to the complete, all-embracing love that reflects their Father, a goal toward which His children grow.
48.explain:
“Therefore you shall be perfect,”

“Therefore” connects Jesus’ command to His teaching about loving enemies. The Greek word teleios, translated “perfect,” carries the idea of being complete, mature, or fully accomplishing the purpose for which something was made. Something is perfect when it fulfills its intended purpose. God created humanity in His image to reflect His nature and character (Genesis 1:26–27). In calling His disciples to be perfect, Jesus is calling them to fulfill God’s purpose: to be like Him and to reflect the Father’s love to creation.

“just as your Father in heaven is perfect.”

The Father Himself is the pattern of this perfection. Jesus has just described His love, which reaches both the righteous and the unrighteous, even His enemies. He gives sun and rain to the evil and the good alike (5:45), and His love is not limited to those who love Him in return. Jesus calls His disciples to reflect that same complete, wholehearted, impartial love. Luke records the parallel saying as “Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36).
48.notes:
The word appears again when Jesus tells the rich young ruler, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor” (19:21). In both places, the call is to wholehearted devotion.

The Greek Old Testament uses teleios for the Hebrew word translated “blameless,” describing wholehearted devotion to God: “You shall be blameless before the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 18:13; compare Genesis 17:1).

The chapter that commands “love your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:18), quoted in 5:43, opens with the call to be holy as God is holy (Leviticus 19:2). Jesus’ conclusion draws the whole passage back to that chapter’s central concern.
